idiom_name: switch expression over a discriminated record hierarchy (message type as the discriminator)
implementation_notes: C# has no BCL router, so the idiomatic realization is a switch expression over a closed message model - an abstract record with one derived record per message kind - where the runtime type is the discriminator and property patterns express value rules; the compiler warns when the switch stops covering a case, and a final discard arm is the explicit fallback, so no router object or handler registry is written. The classic handler-table form (a Dictionary<Type, Func<Msg, Task>> filled from DI) remains justified when the rule set is configuration-driven, and broker-side rules are the alternative when the decision belongs to the platform.
pitfalls: A switch expression is exhaustive only while the hierarchy is closed and the discard arm is last: adding a message type in another assembly routes everything new into the fallback arm instead of breaking the build.
Property patterns are evaluated in order, so a broad pattern placed before a specific one shadows it; the compiler reports subsumed arms, not wrong business precedence.
A router that calls .Result/.Wait() on the send deadlocks under a SynchronizationContext: make the dispatcher async all the way (Task Route) rather than blocking inside a synchronous handler.

variants.name: Broker-side subscription rules (Azure Service Bus topic filters)
variants.implementation_notes: Push the decision into the broker: each destination becomes a subscription on one topic and its rules - SqlFilter("color = 'blue' AND quantity = 10") or the cheaper CorrelationFilter - decide which messages that subscription receives, so no application-side router component exists at all. Know the verified limitation before choosing this form: Service Bus filters evaluate message and system properties and cannot evaluate the message body, so a body-based decision must be promoted to an application property by the producer or implemented in-process instead. Replace each subscription's default TrueFilter rule (which selects everything) and prefer correlation filters over SQL filters when the conditions allow, because SQL rules cost throughput.
pitfalls: SQL filters cannot read the message body - only properties and system properties - so 'content-based' here means 'property-based': the discriminator must be promoted at publish time or the rule never matches.
Rules without actions are OR-ed into a single delivery while each rule with an action produces its own copy, so how many copies a subscription receives depends on how the rules are written.
Forgetting to remove the default TrueFilter rule makes the subscription receive the entire stream; SQL filters also reduce overall throughput compared with correlation filters (documented cost).
